summary: This informational document shows how Segment Routing can solve the BGP Egress Peer Engineering requirement. In this design a centralized SDN controller can program any egress peer policy at ingress border routers or at hosts within the domain.

plainLanguage.summary: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) normally picks the best path to a destination by itself. This RFC shows how a central controller can override that choice for specific traffic. The router that holds the external connections gives each peer, link or group of peers a number, tells the controller about those numbers, and the controller then tells the entry router to push the right list of numbers so the traffic leaves through the chosen peer.

questions: segment routing bgp egress peer engineering
what is bgp egress peer engineering
how does segment routing enable centralized traffic engineering
how does bgp-ls advertise topology to the controller
subtitle: Letting a central controller steer traffic out of a network through a chosen border router and a chosen external peer.

tldr.problem: An operator may want a central controller to decide which border router and which external peer a flow leaves the network through, instead of letting BGP pick the best path on its own.
tldr.mechanism: The border router that holds the external peers allocates BGP Peering SIDs for its peers, links and peer sets, and advertises them to the controller over BGP-LS. The controller then programs the ingress router or the source host with a segment list made of the egress router's Prefix-SID and the chosen Peering SID.
tldr.outcome: Traffic can be steered to a chosen exit point without new capabilities at the ingress router and without per-route labels. The document describes an architecture and leaves the controller definition and the full programming methods out of scope.

today: RFC 9087 is an Informational RFC published in August 2021 and has not been obsoleted. The BGP-LS extensions it relies on are specified in RFC 9086. The document describes an architecture: the definition of the controller itself and the exhaustive list of ways to program a policy are both stated to be outside its scope.

sections.title: The Egress Peer Engineering Problem
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) lets a node steer a packet through a chosen set of instructions, called segments, by prepending the packet with an SR header. A segment can be any instruction, topological or service based. SR allows a flow to be enforced along any topological path while keeping per-flow state only at the ingress node of the SR domain. The architecture applies directly to the MPLS data plane with no change to the forwarding plane, and needs only a minor extension to the existing link-state routing protocols.

The document applies Segment Routing to the BGP Egress Peer Engineering (BGP-EPE) requirement, whose problem statement is defined in RFC 7855. A centralized controller should be able to instruct an ingress Provider Edge (PE) router, or a content source inside the domain, to use a specific egress PE and a specific external interface or neighbour to reach a particular destination. The controller is called the BGP-EPE controller, the border router where the steering is implemented is called a BGP-EPE-enabled border router, and the input policy programmed at the ingress border router or source host is called a BGP-EPE policy.

The requirements that motivated the solution are listed in the text. The solution MUST apply to the Internet use case, where Internet routes are assumed to be IPv4 unlabeled or IPv6 unlabeled, and it is not required to place those routes in a VPN Routing and Forwarding instance or to allocate labels per route or per path. It MUST support any deployed Internal BGP scheme, such as route reflectors, confederations or full meshes, and MUST apply to routers with both external and internal peers. It should minimize the need for new BGP capabilities at the ingress PEs, and MUST accommodate an ingress BGP-EPE policy at an ingress PE or directly at a source inside the domain. It MAY support automated Fast Reroute and fast convergence mechanisms.

The worked example uses a four-AS topology. Router C sits in AS1 with three external peers: D in AS2, and E and F in AS3, the last reached over a multi-hop session. X is the BGP-EPE controller inside AS1 and H is a content source inside AS1. For editorial reasons the example is written with IPv6 addresses and MPLS SIDs; the same solution applies to IPv4 with MPLS SIDs and to IPv6 with native IPv6 SIDs.
sections.plainLanguage: Segment Routing works by putting a list of instructions on the front of a packet, so the sender decides where it goes rather than each router. This RFC applies that idea to the exit point of a network: a central controller can order traffic to leave through one border router and one particular external neighbour, instead of letting the border gateway protocol decide on its own.

sections.title: BGP Peering Segments
sections.content:
As defined in RFC 8402, certain segments are defined by a BGP-EPE-capable node and correspond to its attached peers. These are called BGP Peering Segments or BGP Peering SIDs, and they let an inter-domain path be expressed as a source-routed instruction list.

An ingress border router of an AS composes a list of segments to steer a flow along a selected path inside the AS, towards a selected egress border router, and out through a specific peer. At minimum a BGP-EPE policy involves two segments: the Node SID of the chosen egress router, then the BGP Peering Segment for the chosen peer or peering interface.

Three types of BGP Peering Segment are defined. A Peer Node Segment describes a peer. A Peer Adjacency Segment describes a link. A Peer Set Segment describes a link or a node that is part of a set.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of number can be attached to the outside world of a router. One names a neighbour, one names a particular link to a neighbour, and one names a group of neighbours or links. Putting a number in the segment list tells the network to leave by that neighbour, by that link, or by any member of that group.

sections.title: Allocating and Advertising the Peering SIDs
sections.content:
Working in a ships-in-the-night mode with respect to the pre-existing iBGP design, a BGP-LS session is established between the BGP-EPE-enabled border router and the BGP-EPE controller. From its local configuration, and following the behaviour described in RFC 9086, node C allocates a PeerNode segment for each of its defined peers (1012 for D, 1022 for E and 1052 for F), a PeerAdj segment for each recursing interface to a multi-hop peer (the upper and lower interfaces from C to F in the example), and a PeerSet segment for the set of peers E and F, which belong to the same AS.

C programs its forwarding table accordingly. Each incoming label pops and selects an outgoing interface: 1012 goes to the link to D, 1022 to the link to E, 1032 to the upper link to F, 1042 to the lower link to F, 1052 load balances over any link to F, and 1060 load balances over any link to E or to F.

C then signals each related BGP-LS instance of Network Layer Reachability Information to the controller. Each route carries descriptors and attributes. The PeerNode route to D, for example, has local node descriptors 192.0.2.3, AS1 and BGP-LS Identifier 1000, remote node descriptors 192.0.2.4 and AS2, link descriptors 2001:db8:cd::c and 2001:db8:cd::d, and the attribute PeerNode SID 1012. The routes to E and to F add the PeerSetSID 1060, and the two PeerAdj routes to F carry the attributes PeerAdj-SID 1032 and PeerAdj-SID 1042 with their own link descriptors.

Two notes complete the mechanism. The manageability functions of BGP-LS also apply to the extensions this use case requires, and further manageability considerations are described in RFC 9086. On security, BGP-LS defines the NLRI instances and their associated security aspects, and the BGP-LS extensions required by BGP-EPE include the related security as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The border router that owns the external connections picks the numbers, installs them in its own forwarding table so that each number sends traffic out of the right interface, and then tells the controller about them over a link-state session carried in BGP.

sections.title: Fast Reroute for Peering SIDs
sections.content:
A BGP-EPE-enabled border router MAY allocate a Fast Reroute backup entry on a per-BGP-Peering-SID basis. For a PeerNode SID the order is: if the peer is multi-hop, back up via the remaining PeerAdj SIDs, if available, to the same peer; otherwise back up via another PeerNode SID to the same AS; otherwise pop the PeerNode SID and perform an IP lookup. For a PeerAdj SID the order is: if the peer is multi-hop, back up via the remaining PeerAdj SIDs to the same peer; otherwise back up via a PeerNode SID to the same AS; otherwise pop the PeerNode SID and perform an IP lookup. For a PeerSet SID, back up via the remaining PeerNode SIDs in the same PeerSet, otherwise pop the PeerNode SID and do an IP lookup.

The example shows what each rule means. If the upper CF link fails, C can reroute all traffic for PeerNode SID 1052 onto the lower CF link to the same peer F. If the CE link fails, C can reroute all traffic for PeerNode SID 1022 onto the link to PeerNode SID 1052, that is to F. If the CD link fails, C can pop the PeerNode SID and look up the IP destination address in its forwarding table. If a link inside the group fails, traffic for PeerSet SID 1060 is rerouted onto any other member of the group.

The operator keeps the last word. For business reasons the default behaviour may not be wanted, so the operator should be able to associate a specific backup PeerNode SID with a PeerNode SID: SID 1022 for peer E could be required to be backed up by SID 1012 for peer D, overruling the default that would have preferred F.
sections.plainLanguage: Each peering number comes with a fallback order for when the link fails. The router prefers another link to the same neighbour, then another neighbour in the same autonomous system, and only as a last resort falls back to looking up the destination address normally. An operator who needs a specific fallback can override the default.

sections.title: What the Controller Collects and Decides
sections.content:
The document lists a non-exhaustive set of inputs the BGP-EPE controller would collect to make its decision. The exhaustive definition is out of scope.

  • Valid paths from peers. The controller collects all the BGP paths, that is the IP destination prefixes, advertised by the BGP-EPE-enabled border routers. This could be an iBGP session with the router configured to advertise all paths using BGP ADD-PATH with the original next hop preserved, so that the controller learns, for example, that C reaches 2001:db8:abcd::/48 through neighbour 2001:db8:cd::d of AS2, through 2001:db8:ce::e of AS3, or through 2001:db8:f::f of AS3. An alternative is for a collector to track the Adj-RIB-In of the border routers with the BGP Monitoring Protocol.
  • Intra-domain topology. The internal topology and the related IGP SIDs, collected from the IGP Link-State Database of each area or through a BGP-LS session with a node in each IGP area.
  • External topology. From the BGP-LS routes of Section 3, the controller keeps an accurate description of the egress topology of node C and can associate BGP Peering SIDs with the components of that topology.
  • SLA characteristics of each peer. Measuring service level agreements across peers requires a BGP-EPE solution, because the probes have to be steered via non-best-path peers. Unidirectional monitoring of the desired path is likely required, which dissociates the return path from the forward path, since the return path usually cannot be controlled.
  • Traffic matrix. The traffic matrix to the peers or the final destinations, with IPFIX a likely option, or the link utilization statistics of the internal and external links.
  • Business policies. Configured or collected through any desired mechanism; those mechanisms are out of scope.

On the basis of these and likely other inputs, the controller decides to steer some demands away from their best BGP path. The policy is likely expressed as a two-entry segment list, the first element being the IGP Prefix-SID of the selected egress border router and the second a BGP Peering SID at that border router. The examples in the document are: prefer egress router C and peer AS2, {64, 1012}, where 64 is the SID of router C; prefer egress router C and peer AS3 via eBGP peer 2001:db8:ce::e, {64, 1022}; prefer egress router C and peer AS3 via eBGP peer 2001:db8:f::f, {64, 1052}; prefer egress router C and peer AS3 via interface 2001:db8:cf2::f of the multi-hop eBGP peer, {64, 1042}; and prefer egress router C and any interface to any peer in group 1060, {64, 1060}. The first SID may also be replaced by a list of segments when an explicit path inside the domain is required, for example {60, 64, 1012} to steer traffic from A to C via B and then out to peer D.
sections.plainLanguage: Before choosing an exit the controller gathers what it needs: which destinations each border router can reach and by which neighbour, the internal topology, the measured quality of each neighbour's path, the traffic volumes involved, and the operator's business rules. The result is normally two numbers: which border router to leave by, and which neighbour to leave to.

sections.title: Programming the Input Policy
sections.content:
The exhaustive description of the ways to implement a BGP-EPE policy is out of scope, but the document gives several examples.

At a host. A static IP/MPLS route can be programmed at the host, defining a destination prefix, a next hop and a label stack to push. Assuming the same Segment Routing Global Block on at least all access routers connecting the hosts, the same policy can be programmed across all hosts.

At a router, using a Segment Routing traffic-engineering tunnel. The controller configures the ingress border router with a tunnel and a steering policy that maps a class of traffic onto that tunnel, and the tunnel pushes the required segment list. The tunnel and the steering policy could be configured with PCEP, with NETCONF, or through other static or ephemeral APIs. The example at router A is a tunnel T1 pushing {64, 1042}, with the IP route L/8 set to next hop T1.

At a router, using a unicast route labeled with BGP. The controller builds a unicast route from scratch and sends it to the ingress router. The route needs the destination prefix to engineer, for example L/8; the next hop, which is the selected egress border router C; a label, which is the selected egress peer 1042; and the AS path of the selected valid AS path. Some BGP policy is needed to make the ingress router choose it as best. Comparing a labeled and an unlabeled unicast BGP route is implementation dependent, so an implementation-specific policy may be needed on each ingress router. Such a route overwrites an equivalent or less specific best path, which means the option can influence the path propagated to upstream peers and customers; implementations that treat SAFI-1 and SAFI-4 routes for a prefix as comparable would trigger a BGP WITHDRAW of the SAFI-1 route to their upstream peers.

At a router, using a VPN policy route. The controller builds a VPNv4 route from scratch with the destination prefix, the next hop pointing at the egress border router, the label of the selected egress peer, a route target selecting the appropriate VRF instance at the ingress router, and the AS path of the selected valid AS path, plus BGP policy to make it best in that VRF. The VRF instance must be preconfigured, and a VRF fallback to the main forwarding table may be beneficial so that normal Internet paths do not have to be replicated in every VRF.

The document then lists the benefits: no assumption about the iBGP design inside AS1; next-hop-self on the Internet routes propagated to the ingress border routers remains possible, which is a common rule to minimize the number of IGP routes and to avoid importing external churn into the internal routing domain; consistent support for traffic engineering inside the domain and at its external edge; support for programming the policy at a host as well as at an ingress border router; and no new functionality needed at the ingress router, since BGP-EPE is only required on the BGP-EPE-enabled egress border router and the controller. The same input policy can also be deployed across hosts connected to different routers, assuming the global property of IGP Prefix-SIDs.
sections.plainLanguage: The chosen pair of numbers has to reach the place where the traffic enters the domain. It can be pushed as a static route on the sending host, as a traffic-engineering tunnel on the entry router, as a labelled BGP route, or as a private VPN route. In every case the entry router just needs to push the two numbers, and it needs no new protocol features to do it.

items.title: Valid paths from peers
items.text: The prefixes each border router advertises, and the neighbour each path arrives from.

items.title: Intra-domain topology
items.text: The internal topology and the related IGP SIDs.

items.title: External topology
items.text: The egress topology of each border router, with its peering SIDs.

items.title: SLA characteristics
items.text: Measured service level agreement per peer, which needs probes steered off the best path.

items.title: Traffic matrix
items.text: Traffic volumes towards peers or final destinations, or link utilization statistics.

items.title: Business policies
items.text: The operator's own rules, configured or collected by some other mechanism.
